verses.text: Rhea wrapped a great stone in baby clothes and handed it
to Cronus, son of Ouranos, the mighty lord who then ruled the gods.
He took it in his hands and swallowed it into his belly,
the ruthless creature. He never realized that, left behind,
his own son, unconquerable and untroubled, was safe in place of the stone,
and would soon overpower him with his strength and his own hands,
drive him from his royal honors, and himself rule among the immortals.
Then the young lord Zeus's strength and splendid limbs
grew swiftly. As the years rolled on,
tricked by Gaia's deeply knowing advice,
great Cronus, with his crooked schemes, brought his children back up,
overcome by the cunning and strength of his own son.
First he vomited out the stone he had swallowed last.
Zeus set it firmly in the earth with its broad roads,
at holy Pytho, in the valleys beneath Parnassus,
to stand as a sign for ages to come, a wonder for mortal people.
Zeus freed his father's brothers from their terrible chains,
the sons of Ouranos, whom their father had recklessly bound.
They remembered his kindness and repaid his good deeds:
they gave him thunder and the smoking thunderbolt
and lightning, which vast Gaia had kept hidden until then.
Trusting in these weapons, Zeus rules over mortals and immortals.
Iapetus took as his wife a daughter of Oceanus with lovely ankles,
Clymene, and went to bed with her.
She bore him a son, Atlas, strong in spirit,
and Menoetius, full of overbearing pride, and Prometheus,
clever and endlessly inventive, and Epimetheus, whose thinking went astray.
From the start, Epimetheus brought trouble to people who live on bread:
he was the first to welcome the woman Zeus had fashioned,
a virgin. As for violent Menoetius, Zeus, whose gaze reaches far,
struck him with a smoking thunderbolt and sent him down into Erebus,
because of his recklessness and overpowering arrogance.
Atlas holds up the broad sky under harsh compulsion,
at the ends of the earth, before the clear-voiced Hesperides,
standing with the weight on his head and tireless hands.
This was the fate Zeus, the wise planner, assigned him.
Zeus bound Prometheus, with all his intricate schemes, in inescapable
and painful chains, driving a pillar through his middle.
He set a long-winged eagle on him, and it ate his liver,
which could not die. The liver grew back fully
each night, as much as the wide-winged bird had eaten all day.
Heracles, mighty son of Alcmene with her lovely ankles,
killed the eagle and drove that cruel affliction
away from Prometheus, son of Iapetus, freeing him from his suffering,
with the consent of Zeus, who rules on high from Olympus,
so that the fame of Heracles, born in Thebes, would grow
still greater than before across the earth that feeds so many.
Out of regard for this, Zeus honored his glorious son.
Angry though he was, Zeus gave up the anger he had long held
because Prometheus had matched wits with him, the mighty son of Cronus.

uncertainties: Verse 496 is marked for deletion in the supplied Greek. It is translated here because every assigned verse requires an entry.
The construction in verse 522 is disputed: it may describe fastening Prometheus to a pillar rather than driving a pillar through his body.
